passage: On Monday the coaching centre's corridor board went up again: names in batches, A at the top, D at the bottom, and Devika's name in D. The announcement came fast: "D batch, you still have time, but the crash course closes Friday." Devika's chest tightened all evening, and the pile of notes looked like a wall. At dinner Devika pushed rice around the plate. Manjula Mausi, visiting from Pune, asked what was wrong. "They keep saying D batch like it's an illness," Devika said. "And then the crash course pops up." Devika stopped. "They need us scared." Mausi said nothing, only nodded. Next morning Devika wrote a plan at a steady pace and said Papa would see it too.

qa.q: Which batch was Devika's name in on the corridor board?
qa.a: Devika's name was in D, the bottom batch.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling on the evening after the board went up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Devika felt anxious and small; the tightened chest, the wall of notes and the pushed-around rice show it.

qa.q: What small step would help Devika if the fear comes back?
qa.a: Keep to the steady plan, remember the board is part of how the centre sells its crash course, and talk to Manjula Mausi or Papa if Devika starts to crumble.

qa.q: How might the coaching centre see the ranking board?
qa.a: As a way to sell fear and the crash course to families; Devika's remark that the crash course pops up right after the batches points that way.

grounding: A coaching centre ranks students in batches and sells the crash course; Devika notices this and goes at own pace with adult support.

passage:
Tuesday

The coaching centre put up the new batch list today. I've been moved from A to C. They read the names out loud. In the C room, the instructor said, "Welcome to the back benches. Unless you take the weekend crash course, forget about a good college." Then a man from the office came round with forms for the crash course.

I felt like dirt. Salma got moved to C as well, and she cried in the stairwell.

But on the bus, I kept thinking about the forms. They move you down, make you scared, then sell you the fix. That's not about me. That's how they make money.

My mock marks went up ten points this month, which the list doesn't say.

I'm still shaky. When I got home, I told Amma everything, even the part about feeling like dirt. She listened and then said, "We'll go and talk to them together, and we'll decide about the crash course later, not tonight." I slept better than I have in weeks.

Ramesh

qa.q: Which batch was Ramesh moved to?
qa.a: Ramesh was moved from A to C.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the instructor spoke in the C room?
qa.a: Ramesh felt humiliated and worthless, like dirt, after being labelled a back-bencher.

qa.q: What did Ramesh notice on the bus, and why does it help?
qa.a: Ramesh noticed the centre moves students down, scares them and then sells a crash course, which helps Ramesh see the fear as a sales tactic rather than the truth.

qa.q: How might Salma feel about the batch list?
qa.a: Salma seems hurt and humiliated too, since she cried in the stairwell after being moved to C.

grounding: It shows a teen ranked down by a coaching centre that uses fear to sell courses, who sees the business model, keeps their own progress in view and talks to a trusted adult.
